situation:
You are the marketing coordinator at TIDEWATER SWIM AND DIVE CLUB, a family business now in its third generation. The club president (judge), the founder's granddaughter, has asked you to recommend how the club should sell the sponsorship inventory it leaves unsold every season, and to explain what that change would mean for the sponsors who have been with the club longest.

The club runs eleven meets a year at its own pool and sells sponsorships for lane banners, program pages, and the scoreboard. The club president (judge) writes every sponsorship letter and every renewal invoice by hand, one at a time, to about sixty local businesses. Sponsors say in every survey that the letters are why they renew, and three of them have sponsored the club for more than twenty years.

About a third of the inventory still goes unsold, roughly forty thousand dollars a season, because the letters cannot reach every prospect before the meets begin. A sponsorship platform would send templated email offers to a purchased list of four hundred regional businesses and post payments straight into the club's accounting software, and the vendor projects the club would fill the inventory within two seasons.

Adopting the platform ends the hand-written letters. Every sponsor would receive the same template the platform sends for every club that uses it, and the longtime sponsors renew on a relationship the club would be handing to software. Keeping the letters keeps that relationship and leaves a third of the inventory unsold, which is the forty thousand dollars a season the club had planned to put toward resurfacing the diving well.

The club president (judge) wants your recommendation on whether to adopt the platform or keep writing the letters by hand, and on how you would put that case in writing to the sponsors it affects. The club president (judge) will greet you in the office and ask to hear your ideas. After you have presented and answered the questions, the club president (judge) will thank you for your work.
